What is TypeScript and why use it over JavaScript?

TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript that adds static types and compiles (transpiles) to plain JS. It catches type errors at compile time, enables reliable refactoring and IDE autocomplete, and documents intent in code. Types are erased at runtime, so it adds no runtime overhead — but also no runtime validation, so data from APIs still needs checking where it matters.
Interface vs type alias — what is the difference?

Both can describe object shapes and both can be extended (extends vs &). Only interfaces support declaration merging and are slightly clearer in error messages for objects. Only type aliases can represent unions, tuples, primitives, mapped and conditional types. 💡 A common rule: interfaces for object contracts/DTOs, types for unions and compositions — and be consistent.
What is the difference between any, unknown and never?

any disables type checking — you can do anything with it, and it silently spreads. unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow (typeof, type guard) before using it, so it is the safe choice for untrusted data. never represents values that cannot exist: a function that always throws, or the leftover type in an exhaustive switch.

What is a discriminated union?

A union of object types that share a common literal property (the discriminant), such as status: 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'. Switching on that property narrows to the exact member, so TS knows which fields exist. Adding a never default case gives an exhaustiveness check — the compiler errors if a new variant is added but not handled. It is ideal for modelling UI or request state.
Explain generics and generic constraints.

Generics parameterise types so code is reusable yet type-safe: function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined returns the element type of whatever array you pass. Constraints restrict what T can be: <T extends { id: number }> guarantees T has an id; <K extends keyof T> guarantees a valid key. Unlike Java there is no type at runtime at all, so you cannot do new T() or instanceof T.
Name some utility types and when you'd use them.

Partial<T> for update/PATCH payloads or form values; Omit<T, 'id'> for create DTOs; Pick<T, K> for list-view projections; Readonly<T> for immutable state; Record<K, V> for lookup maps; ReturnType<typeof fn> to derive types from functions; NonNullable<T> to strip null/undefined. They are built on mapped and conditional types.
Enum vs string literal union — which do you prefer?

A literal union (type Status = 'ACTIVE' | 'INACTIVE') has no runtime footprint, matches JSON from a Spring backend directly and gives the same autocomplete and safety. Enums create a runtime object, which is useful when you need to iterate values or want a namespace, but numeric enums accept any number and add bundle weight. Many teams prefer unions plus const STATUSES = ['ACTIVE', 'INACTIVE'] as const when runtime values are needed.
What does strict mode enable, and why is strictNullChecks important?

"strict": true turns on noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictPropertyInitialization, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, alwaysStrict and useUnknownInCatchVariables. With strictNullChecks, null and undefined are not assignable to other types, so you must handle them explicitly — eliminating most "cannot read property of undefined" bugs. 💡 New Angular projects enable strict mode by default; keep it on.
What are the optional chaining, nullish coalescing and non-null assertion operators?

user?.address?.city short-circuits to undefined if any part is null/undefined. value ?? 'default' uses the default only for null/undefined (unlike ||, which also replaces 0 and ''). value! tells the compiler "trust me, not null" — it does nothing at runtime, so overusing it hides bugs.
What are decorators and how does Angular use them?

Decorators are functions applied with @ that annotate classes or members with metadata or wrap behaviour. Angular's compiler reads @Component, @Injectable, @Directive, @Pipe metadata to generate code, and member decorators like @Input, @Output, @ViewChild, @HostListener wire up bindings. In Angular 17+ many member decorators have signal-based function equivalents (input(), output(), viewChild()) and DI can use inject().
Is TypeScript's private really private?

No — private and protected are enforced only by the compiler; after compilation the field is a normal JS property accessible via obj['field']. JavaScript's native #field syntax is enforced at runtime. For Angular templates, note that private members cannot be used in the template; use protected for template-only members.
What is structural typing?

TS checks compatibility by shape, not by declared name. If an object has all required properties of an interface, it is assignable to it even if it never "implements" it. This differs from Java's nominal typing. One nuance: object literals passed directly get excess property checks, so extra unknown properties are flagged.
What does keyof and typeof do in a type position?

keyof T produces a union of T's property names (keyof Patient → 'id' | 'name' | 'email'). typeof value in a type position extracts the type of a variable, so you can derive types from runtime constants: type Route = typeof routes[keyof typeof routes]. Combined with indexed access types (T[K]) they enable type-safe helpers.

What are declaration files (.d.ts)?

They contain only type information (no implementation) describing the shape of JavaScript code, so TS can type-check usage of plain JS libraries. Many libraries ship their own; others have community types in @types/* (e.g. @types/node). You can also write declare module 'x' or augment existing types via declaration merging.
Type annotation vs "as" assertion vs "satisfies": what is the difference?

An annotation (const c: Config = {…}) checks the value and then the variable has the wider declared type, losing literal details. An assertion ({…} as Config) tells the compiler "trust me"; it skips most checks and can hide bugs, such as a missing property. satisfies ({…} satisfies Config) checks the value against the type but keeps the inferred, narrower type, so you get both validation and precise autocomplete. Prefer annotations or satisfies; keep as for cases where you know more than the compiler, such as DOM element types.

What is a type predicate (x is T) and what is the risk?

A function returning x is T tells the compiler that when it returns true, the argument has type T. It lets you narrow unknown data such as a parsed JSON body or a caught error. The risk is that TypeScript does not verify the body: a guard that only checks one property will happily "prove" a wrong type. Keep guards small and tested, or use a schema library for complex shapes.
Does http.get<Patient[]>() validate the response? How do you keep front-end and Spring DTOs in sync?

No. The generic only casts the parsed JSON; nothing is checked at runtime. To catch drift: generate TypeScript models from the Spring Boot OpenAPI document in CI, so a renamed field breaks the build; validate critical responses with a schema (Zod) and report mismatches; and remember that Java LocalDate/Instant arrive as strings, and large long IDs can lose precision as JavaScript numbers, so type them as string when needed.
Abstract class vs interface in TypeScript?

An interface is compile-time only: it describes a shape, produces no JavaScript, and a class can implement many. An abstract class exists at runtime, can hold shared implementation, constructors and fields, and declares abstract members that subclasses must implement; a class can extend only one. In Angular, an abstract class is also useful as a DI token ({ provide: PaymentGateway, useClass: StripeGateway }), because interfaces vanish at runtime and cannot be tokens.
Index signature vs Record vs Map: which do you use for a lookup table?

{ [key: string]: number } and Record<string, number> are equivalent for open string keys; Record<'A' | 'B', number> requires exactly those keys, which is great for exhaustive lookups. Note that by default obj[key] on an open index signature is typed as number, not number | undefined; enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess to be honest about missing keys. Use a Map when keys are not strings, when entries are added and removed often, or when insertion order and size matter.
What does distributive conditional type mean? Give an example where it surprises people.

When a conditional type checks a bare type parameter, a union argument is split and each member is checked separately: type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never turns string | number into string[] | number[], not (string | number)[]. To prevent distribution, wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never. This is also why Exclude and Extract work on unions.
const vs readonly vs Readonly<T> vs as const?

| const | readonly | Readonly<T> | as const
Applies to | A variable binding | One property or array type | All top-level properties of a type | A literal expression
Stops | Reassigning the variable | Assigning that property | Assigning any top-level property | Any change, deeply, and widening
Contents mutable? | Yes (p.name = 'x' works) | Nested objects yes | Nested objects yes | No (all readonly)
Exists at run time | Yes (JavaScript) | No | No | No
const roles = ['ADMIN', 'DOCTOR'] as const;
type Role = typeof roles[number];   // 'ADMIN' | 'DOCTOR'
Rule of thumb: const is about the variable, the others are about the type. None of the type-level ones freeze the object at run time; use Object.freeze for that.
Optional property (name?: string) vs name: string | undefined?

| name?: string | name: string | undefined
Key may be missing | Yes | No, it must be written
Reading gives | string | undefined | string | undefined
Object literal { } | Allowed | Error: property missing
Explicit undefined | Allowed (unless exactOptionalPropertyTypes is on) | Allowed
Good for | Fields a form or API may omit | Forcing callers to decide, even if the answer is "none"
Rule of thumb: use ? for genuinely optional data; use the explicit union when forgetting the field would be a bug.
Class method vs arrow-function property in an Angular component?

| save() { } | save = () => { }
Stored | Once, on the prototype | On every instance
this when passed as a callback | Lost (no longer the component) | Always the component
Override in a subclass and call super | Yes | No super.save()
Called from a template | Works | Works
setTimeout(this.save, 0);          // method: this is lost
setTimeout(() => this.save(), 0);  // safe either way
Rule of thumb: write normal methods and wrap them in an arrow at the call site when you pass them around; use an arrow property only for handlers handed to third-party code.
null vs undefined when Angular talks to a Spring Boot API?

| null | undefined
Meaning | "Has no value" (set on purpose) | "Was never set" or key absent
In JSON | Valid value: "dob": null | Not valid; the key is dropped by JSON.stringify
From Jackson | Default for null Java fields | When @JsonInclude(NON_NULL) omits the field
typeof | "object" | "undefined"
Safe check | x == null or x ?? fallback catch both | Same
Interview tip: for PATCH-style updates the difference matters: a missing key means "leave it", while null means "clear it". Agree on this with the back end and type the DTO accordingly.
